newsitem.title: MEXICO: Foreign stockpickers boost Mexico banks - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Foreign stockpickers boost Mexico banks - analysts.

text.p: Long-neglected Mexican financial stocks have rocketed in recent weeks and far outpaced even the record-breaking Mexican bourse as foreign investors have decided to return to the sector, analysts say.
Nonetheless, stockwatchers urge caution over the cheap but risky sector's near-term outlook as the market awaits a possible sector-wide plan to restructure mortgages.

For Robert Lacoursiere of Santander Investment in Mexico, the financials -- as stocks in financial services companies are known -- had gained after lagging behind the Mexican bourse for most of the year.
Financial groups in Mexico include a major bank as well as other financial service institutions as diverse as brokerages and insurance companies.
Summarizing their recent stock performance, Lacoursiere said, "Financials were very undervalued and started underperforming the market in January, Bancomer in particular."
"Basically foreigners have decided to get back into the (financial) sector over the last month," he added.

Shares listed by Mexico's two biggest financial groups Bancomer and Banacci were still sharply ahead of where they stood at the beginning of June, despite flagging a little in early trade on the Mexican bourse on Wednesday.
"What's happened recently is that foreigners have bought into financials as a leveraged way to play the Mexican recovery," said Enrique Pani, an analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell-Mexico.
"Financials were very cheap in valuation terms, they were trading at below or near to one-times book value," he added.
Bancomer shares, at 3.82 pesos, were up 28.6 percent for the month to date, while Banacci B shares had gained 20.3 percent over the same period.
By comparison, the Mexican Bolsa's blue chip IPC index, had gained 7.3 percent for the month, after notching up nine record closes.
"Both Banacci and Bancomer have done well, but Bancomer has done better as it was cheaper in valuation terms," said Jose Garcia-Cantera, of Salomon Brothers in New York.

The analysts were mixed, but cautious, in their reception to news reports Banacci would introduce on Monday a plan to offer discounts on mortgage debt installments to clients who had not missed recent payments.
The news came after recent market speculation hefty past-due mortgage debts held by the financial groups' banking arms would be restructured with government help.
"There could be some market disappointment the government was not involved, but we think its is a good move in the medium-term," Pani said.
"The trick is to see whether they (Banacci) can bring back past-due clients into current status," he added.
Lacoursiere noted that although Banacci was "taking the bull by the horns," it was not the first bank to have unveiled such a mortgage plan.
"Other banks are doing it already, so what's the fuss?" he said.
"It (the plan) demonstrates mortgages are still a problem, and will be until there is a recovery in purchasing power," he added. "We would like to see some leading indicators showing credit growth."
Garcia-Cantera said the outlook for Mexico's financial groups was less pessimistic than in recent years due to a sharper than expected fall in domestic interest rates coupled with a stable peso.
"The bottom line is that banks are better than they used to be," said Garcia-Cantera said. "Not because the upside has improved, but because the downside is more limited."
